statement: To find two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial and the rectangle contained by them medial and moreover incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them.
heath_proof: Let there be set out two medial straight lines AB, BC commensurable in square only, containing a medial rectangle, and such that the square on AB is greater than the square on BC by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AB; [X. 32, ad fin.]let the semicircle ADB be described on AB, and let the rest of the construction be as above. Then, since AF is incommensurable in length with FB, [X. 18] AD is also incommensurable in square with DB. [X. 11] And, since the square on AB is medial, therefore the sum of the squares on AD, DB is also medial. [III. 31, I. 47] And, since the rectangle AF, FB is equal to the square on each of the straight lines BE, DF, therefore BE is equal to DF; therefore BC is double of FD, so that the rectangle AB, BC is also double of the rectangle AB, FD. But the rectangle AB, BC is medial; therefore the rectangle AB, FD is also medial. [X. 32] And it is equal to the rectangle AD, DB; [Lemma after X. 32] therefore the rectangle AD, DB is also medial. And, since AB is incommensurable in length with BC, while CB is commensurable with BE, therefore AB is also incommensurable in length with BE, [X. 13] so that the square on AB is also incommensurable with the rectangle AB, BE. [X. 11] But the squares on AD, DB are equal to the square on AB, [I. 47] and the rectangle AB, FD, that is, the rectangle AD, DB, is equal to the rectangle AB, BE; therefore the sum of the squares on AD, DB is incommensurable with the rectangle AD, DB. Therefore two straight lines AD, DB incommensurable in square have been found which make the sum of the squares on them medial and the rectangle contained by them medial and moreover incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them.

10.35
**Statement:** To find two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial and the rectangle contained by them medial and moreover incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them.

**Step 1.** Let there be set out two medial straight lines AB, BC commensurable in square only, containing a medial rectangle, and such that the square on the greater, AB, is greater than the square on the less, BC, by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AB [10.32; the remark with which that proposition closes furnishes precisely this variant, in which the excess is the square on a straight line incommensurable with the greater]. Since AB, BC are commensurable in square only, AB is incommensurable in length with BC [D10.1.2]; and since the square on AB exceeds the square on BC, AB is greater than BC.

**Step 2.** Let BC be bisected at F [1.10]. Then BC is double of BF, so the square on BC is four times the square on BF; that is, the square on BF is the fourth part of the square on BC. Since BC is less than AB, BF is less than the half of AB, so the square on BF does not exceed the square described on the half of AB. Therefore let there be applied to AB a parallelogram equal to the square on BF and deficient by a square figure [6.28]; let it be the rectangle contained by AE, EB, the point E lying on AB.

**Step 3.** AB, BC are two unequal straight lines, the square on the greater AB is greater than the square on the less BC by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AB, and to AB there has been applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on BC and deficient by a square figure, dividing AB into AE, EB; therefore AE is incommensurable in length with EB [10.18].

**Step 4.** Let AB be bisected at G [1.10], and with centre G and distance GA let the semicircle ADB be described on AB [P3]; from E let ED be drawn at right angles to AB, meeting the semicircle at D [1.11]; and let AD, DB be joined [P1]. Since the angle ADB is in a semicircle, it is right [3.31].

**Step 5.** In the right-angled triangle ADB the perpendicular DE has been drawn from the right angle to the base AB; therefore the triangles ADE, DBE are similar to the whole triangle ADB and to one another [6.8]. Hence: (a) as BA is to AD, so is AD to AE, so that the square on AD is equal to the rectangle BA, AE [6.17]; (b) as AB is to BD, so is BD to BE, so that the square on BD is equal to the rectangle AB, BE [6.17]; (c) as AE is to ED, so is ED to EB, so that the square on ED is equal to the rectangle AE, EB [6.17]; (d) as AB is to BD, so is AD to DE, so that the rectangle AB, DE is equal to the rectangle AD, DB [6.16].

**Step 6.** The rectangles BA, AE and AB, BE have the same height AB; therefore, as AE is to EB, so is the rectangle BA, AE to the rectangle AB, BE [6.1]. But AE is incommensurable in length with EB (Step 3); therefore the rectangle BA, AE is incommensurable with the rectangle AB, BE [10.11], that is, the square on AD is incommensurable with the square on DB (Step 5a, 5b). Therefore AD, DB are incommensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 7.** Since the angle ADB is right, the squares on AD, DB together are equal to the square on AB [1.47]. But AB is medial, so the square on AB is a medial area; therefore the sum of the squares on AD, DB is medial.

**Step 8.** The square on ED is equal to the rectangle AE, EB (Step 5c), which is equal to the square on BF (Step 2); and since squares on unequal straight lines are unequal, ED is equal to BF. Hence BC is double of ED. Now the rectangles AB, BC and AB, DE have the same height AB, so that, as BC is to DE, so is the rectangle AB, BC to the rectangle AB, DE [6.1]; therefore the rectangle AB, BC is double of the rectangle AB, DE. Thus these two rectangles have to one another the ratio which the number 2 has to the number 1, and they are commensurable [10.6].

**Step 9.** The rectangle AB, BC is medial (Step 1), and the rectangle AB, DE is commensurable with it (Step 8); therefore the rectangle AB, DE is medial [10.23, Por.]. But the rectangle AB, DE is equal to the rectangle AD, DB (Step 5d); therefore the rectangle AD, DB is medial.

**Step 10.** The square on AB and the rectangle AB, BC have the same height AB; therefore, as AB is to BC, so is the square on AB to the rectangle AB, BC [6.1]. But AB is incommensurable in length with BC (Step 1); therefore the square on AB is incommensurable with the rectangle AB, BC [10.11].

**Step 11.** The rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rectangle AB, DE (Step 8) and incommensurable with the square on AB (Step 10); therefore the rectangle AB, DE is incommensurable with the square on AB [10.13]. But the square on AB is equal to the sum of the squares on AD, DB (Step 7), and the rectangle AB, DE is equal to the rectangle AD, DB (Step 5d); therefore the sum of the squares on AD, DB is incommensurable with the rectangle AD, DB.

**Step 12.** Therefore two straight lines AD, DB have been found which are incommensurable in square (Step 6), which make the sum of the squares on them medial (Step 7) and the rectangle contained by them medial (Step 9), and moreover the rectangle incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them (Step 11). Q.E.F.

Note on path: the initial lines are taken from 10.32 (as its closing remark allows) rather than constructed afresh from 10.30, and the equality of the rectangles AB, DE and AD, DB is derived directly from the similar triangles of 6.8 with 6.16, this being the most direct route.
